title: Word Break
statement: Given a string s and a dictionary of words, decide whether s can be cut into a sequence of dictionary words with nothing left over. Words may be reused any number of times, and the dictionary words are distinct.
realWorld: Segmenting text that has no spaces: splitting a run-together hashtag or domain name into words, tokenising Chinese or Japanese where whitespace carries no information, or checking whether a concatenated SKU string decomposes into known component codes.

examples.explanation: cats|and leaves 'og', and cat|sand leaves 'og' too. Several promising starts exist and every one of them dies at the end — which is why the decision cannot be made locally.
a|aab works. Note that grabbing the longest matching word first takes 'aaa' and strands 'b', so a greedy longest-match would wrongly answer false.

constraints: s and the dictionary words are lower-case English letters

bruteForce.idea: Try every first word: for each dictionary word that is a prefix of the remaining string, strip it and recurse on the rest. Succeed when the remainder is empty.

bruteForce.whySlow: Every position is a potential cut, so the recursion explores up to 2^(n-1) ways to chop the string. The waste is that the suffix starting at a given index is re-examined once per way the prefix before it can be cut: on a string like 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaab' with dictionary ['a','aa','aaa'], the question 'can the tail from index 15 be broken?' is asked thousands of times and answered identically every time, because the answer for a suffix cannot depend on how the part before it was split.

patternIdentification: A yes/no question about a whole sequence that decomposes into the same yes/no question about a prefix. State it as a sentence: dp[i] = 'is the prefix of length i breakable?'. The recurrence comes from asking what the last word was — dp[i] is true when there is some split point j < i with dp[j] already true and s[j..i) in the dictionary — so it is an OR over the split point rather than the sum a counting problem would give. Base case: dp[0] = true, because the empty prefix is broken by taking no words at all. The tell that greedy will not do is that a locally attractive piece can strand the remainder: take the longest match in 'aaab' with ['a','aaa','aab'] and you consume 'aaa', leaving an unbreakable 'b', even though a|aab succeeds. Whenever a local choice can be undone only by revisiting it, you need the table, not the heuristic.

optimized.idea: Left to right over prefix lengths, with a boolean table. For each end position i, look back over the possible last words: any j where dp[j] is true and s[j..i) is in the dictionary makes dp[i] true. Bounding j from below by i - (longest dictionary word) means the inner loop is over word lengths, not over the whole string.

commonMistakes: Reaching for a greedy longest-match scan instead of the table. It is fast and it is wrong: 'aaab' with ['a','aaa','aab'] consumes 'aaa' first, cannot break the leftover 'b', and reports false where the answer is true.

Initialising dp[0] = false because 'nothing has been matched yet'. No cell ever becomes true afterwards — dp[i] can only become true by building on an earlier true — so every input, including 'leetcode' with its exact two-word split, returns false.

Writing s.substring(j, i + 1) in the lookup. Java's substring is half-open, so the prefix of length i already ends at index i; the extra character shifts every candidate word by one, the dictionary never matches, and on the final cell the call throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException.
